name: Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Maḍāʾ al-Lakhmī al-Qurṭubī
summary: Andalusian Ẓāhirī judge of the Almohads whose al-Radd ʿalā al-nuḥāt attacked the grammarians' governors, hidden words and second causes: the one great critic of the method of naḥw from within.
bio: Ibn Maḍāʾ was born in Cordoba in 513/1119, studied grammar there (Sībawayh's al-Kitāb among other books) and became chief judge of the Almohad state, whose doctrine followed the literal (Ẓāhirī) school in law.

His al-Radd ʿalā al-nuḥāt, 'the refutation of the grammarians', applies that spirit to grammar. He asks that the theory of the governor (ʿāmil) be dropped, since it is the speaker, not the words, who brings the endings; that grammarians stop supplying hidden words (taqdīr) where nothing is missing from the sense; that they keep the first cause of a rule and drop the second and third causes, which explain nothing a speaker needs; and that they stop setting exercises in words no Arab said. The book was little read until it was printed in the twentieth century, when it was much discussed. He died in Seville in 592/1196.
